planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil as a small specimen tree beneath taller canopy or along a shaded border.

directions: Angyo Dwarf is a compact selection of Japanese snowbell collected in Japan and valued for staying noticeably smaller and denser than the species, usually topping out well under the 20 to 30 foot height typical seedlings reach. In late spring it still carries the species' pendant clusters of small white bell-shaped flowers along its branches, viewed best from below or on a slope where the downward-facing blooms are visible. Its reduced stature makes it a practical choice for smaller shade gardens or under power lines where a full-size snowbell would eventually outgrow the space. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil with shelter from strong wind and harsh midday sun, siting it as an understory tree beneath taller deciduous canopy.
sources: Dirr, M.A. Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

common_name: Showy Mountain Stewartia (Mountain Camellia, Grandiflora Form)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in rich, moisture-retentive, acidic, well-drained soil in dappled shade, taking care not to let the root zone dry out or become compacted during establishment.

directions: This showy form of mountain stewartia, native to the southern Appalachian piedmont and mountains, is distinguished from the typical variety by larger, more substantial white cup-shaped summer flowers with conspicuous reddish-purple stamens at the center, a striking contrast against the white petals. It grows as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with dark green summer foliage that turns orange to red in fall, and mottled, flaking bark that adds winter interest as the plant matures. It is notoriously intolerant of heat, drought, and root disturbance, so it should be planted once and left undisturbed in a cool, humus-rich site with consistent moisture rather than moved or heavily pruned later. Site it as an understory plant in dappled shade with protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, mimicking the cove-forest conditions where it grows wild.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil as a woodland-edge specimen in partial shade; fringetree is slow to establish and resents being moved once settled.

directions: Groenendaal was selected in Belgium for a notably tidier, more structured crown than the loosely rounded, often ungainly habit typical of seedling-grown white fringetree. As a male clone it produces an especially heavy flush of fragrant, strap-petaled white flowers each spring without setting the dark fruit that female and seed-grown trees bear, keeping cleanup minimal beneath the canopy. Its improved form makes it easier to site as a specimen understory tree at the edge of woodland plantings or foundation beds without the sprawling, multi-stemmed sprawl the species can develop. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to light sun, and avoid transplanting established trees since fringetree forms a coarse, slow-to-recover root system.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller canopy; avoid disturbing the root ball once the tree is sited.

directions: Jersey Belle, an old selection originally named by Princeton Nurseries, is grown for extra-large white bell-shaped flowers that densely cover the branches from a young age, heavier flowering than is typical of seedling-grown Carolina silverbells. It carries a narrower, more upright, tiered branching habit than the species, making it a better fit for smaller gardens or tighter planting spaces where a wide-spreading silverbell would not fit. Foliage turns a clear yellow in fall, extending its season of interest beyond the spring bloom. Grow as an understory specimen in humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in partial shade, sheltered from strong wind and intense afternoon sun.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright shade beneath taller canopy; this selection tolerates more shade than many flowering trees of similar size.

directions: Rosy Ridge was selected from the larger-flowered mountain form of Carolina silverbell for clear pink, bell-shaped blossoms that hang in dense clusters along bare branches ahead of spring leaf-out, reading noticeably deeper pink than the long-grown Arnold Pink selection. It performs well in both brighter shade and fuller sun, giving it more siting flexibility than many understory flowering trees, though it still benefits from the cooler root conditions of a partially shaded position. The tree develops a broad, pyramidal habit at maturity and branches low unless trained to a single leader when young. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, acidic soil, watering during dry spells in the first few seasons while the root system establishes.
